nodes.title: Unitary characters extend from open subgroups
nodes.statement: If G is an abelian topological group and U is an open subgroup, every continuous homomorphism U → S¹ is the restriction of a continuous homomorphism G → S¹.
hypotheses: G abelian; U open in G; the character has values in the unit circle. No compactness or finiteness is assumed.
proofSteps: Order extensions by inclusion of their domains and apply Zorn to compatible unions. At a maximal domain D, adjoining x amounts to choosing an n-th root of the prescribed value at xⁿ if a least positive n with xⁿ∈D exists; if no such n exists choose any value. Divisibility of S¹ provides the root, so maximality forces D=G (Dikranjan 2.1.10).
The extended homomorphism is continuous at 1 because its restriction to the open neighbourhood U is continuous. Translate to prove continuity everywhere.

sources.locator: Theorem 2.1.10 and Corollary 2.1.11, pp. 3–4; Lemma 12.3.5(b), p. 90
sources.match: Divisibility gives algebraic character extension; openness upgrades it to continuous extension.

acceptance: For discrete G all subgroups are open.
On 2Z⊂Z a value z at 2 extends by either square root at 1.
Continuity of an algebraic extension is concluded from openness, not from an arbitrary closed domain.

nodes.title: Closed subgroups of real vector groups
nodes.statement: Every closed subgroup H of Rⁿ is V⊕D topologically, where V is a real vector subspace and D is generated over Z by linearly independent vectors in a complementary real subspace. Thus H≅Rˢ×Zᵗ and s+t≤n.
hypotheses: Finite n, usual Euclidean topology; H is closed.
proofSteps: Take a maximal real vector subspace V contained in H and an orthogonal complement V⊥. Then H=V+(H∩V⊥), since subtracting the V-projection stays in H.

If H∩V⊥ were nondiscrete, choose nonzero h_j→0 with h_j/‖h_j‖→u on the compact sphere. For each real a, integers m_j with m_j‖h_j‖→a give m_j h_j→au. Closedness puts Ru in H∩V⊥, contradicting maximality of V.

A discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real vector space is a lattice in its real span: choose a maximal real-linearly independent family from it. Reducing modulo its generated lattice puts each coset in a compact fundamental parallelotope, whose intersection with the discrete subgroup is finite. Thus that lattice has finite index. The subgroup is finitely generated and torsion-free, and finite index preserves its Z-rank, which is the dimension of the real span. A Z-basis is consequently real-linearly independent. Addition V×D→H and its orthogonal projections give the topological product.

sources.locator: Theorem 8.1.2, pp. 51–52; second proof in §8.2, pp. 52–54
sources.match: Closed real subgroups split as a vector space and a discrete lattice. The sketch uses the second proof’s small-vector argument.

acceptance: H=Rⁿ has t=0.
H=Zⁿ has s=0.
A dense proper subgroup of R is outside the closed hypothesis.

nodes.title: Unitary characters extend from closed real subgroups
nodes.statement: Every continuous unitary character of a closed subgroup H≤Rⁿ extends to a continuous unitary character of Rⁿ.
hypotheses: H closed in the finite-dimensional real additive group; target S¹.
proofSteps: Use closed-euclidean-subgroup-structure to write H=V⊕⊕Zj_i.

A continuous character on a real vector group is exp(2πiℓ) for a real linear functional ℓ: lift it through exp:R→S¹ on the simply connected vector space, normalize the lift at zero, and continuity makes the integral defect of additivity zero. On each j_i choose an angle for its prescribed value.
Extend ℓ from V together with those values on the real-linearly independent j_i to Rⁿ by a vector-space basis. Exponentiation gives the extension.

sources.locator: Theorem 8.1.2, pp. 51–52; Example 12.2.4, p. 87, using the lifting Lemma 8.0.7, pp. 50–51
sources.match: The real subgroup structure and the character classification of R give the stated extension by choosing angles on lattice generators.

acceptance: For H=Z the value at 1 may be any point of S¹.
For H=Rⁿ the extension is the original character.
Two choices of lattice angles can give different extensions.

nodes.title: Unitary characters extend from closed compact subgroups
nodes.statement: If K is compact Hausdorff abelian and L≤K is closed, every continuous unitary character of L extends to K.
hypotheses: K compact Hausdorff abelian; L closed, hence compact.
proofSteps: Import CompactGroups Layer 5: irreducible finite-dimensional complex representations of an abelian group are one-dimensional by Schur, and Peter–Weyl gives separation of points by their unitary characters. This separation is obtained after its analytic density proof.
The complex span of restrictions of characters of K is a unital star subalgebra of C(L,C) separating points. The pinned Stone–Weierstrass theorem makes it uniformly dense.

If a character η of L were different from every restricted character, Haar orthogonality would make f↦∫_L conjugate(η)f vanish on this dense span, hence on η itself. Its value on η is 1. Therefore η is a restriction. Use CompactGroups Layer 6 for the normalized Haar character pairing.

sources.locator: Corollary 11.3.4, p. 76; Lemma 12.4.11(a), p. 94
sources.match: Characters extend from compact subgroups. The proof here instead combines the existing Peter–Weyl owner with the pinned Stone–Weierstrass theorem.

acceptance: A character of a finite cyclic subgroup of S¹ extends by an integer power.
For L={1} the trivial character extends.
The separation input is Peter–Weyl, not an unsupported assumption about compact groups.

nodes.title: Extension in groups with a real and compact open subgroup
nodes.statement: Let G be Hausdorff abelian with an open subgroup U topologically isomorphic to Rⁿ×K for compact Hausdorff abelian K. Every continuous unitary character of any closed subgroup H≤G extends to G.
hypotheses: Finite n; specified topological group isomorphism U≅Rⁿ×K; H closed.
proofSteps: Set H₀=H∩U and L=H₀∩({0}×K). Extend the restriction to L by compact-character-extension and divide the given character by that extended K-character.

The resulting character kills L. Projection q:H₀→Rⁿ is closed because K is compact; its image B is closed and the induced H₀/L→B is a topological group isomorphism. Thus the character descends continuously to B. Apply euclidean-character-extension and multiply back by the K-character to extend from H₀ to U.
Glue on H+U using agreement on H∩U. It is an open subgroup and the glued homomorphism is continuous on U. Apply open-subgroup-character-extension to reach G.

sources.locator: Lemma 7.2.3, p. 47 (compact-kernel projection); Lemma 12.3.5(b), p. 90; Lemma 12.4.11(a), p. 94
sources.match: Combining the closed compact projection with compact and open character extension proves the precise class of groups used here, without assuming general Pontryagin duality.

acceptance: n=0 covers groups with a compact open subgroup.
K={1} covers real vector groups and their discrete open extensions.
The image of a closed subgroup under a noncompact-kernel projection can be nonclosed; compactness of K is used.

nodes.title: Unitary characters extend from closed idele subgroups
nodes.statement: For a number field F, every continuous unitary character of a closed subgroup H of A_F× extends to A_F×.
hypotheses: F a number field; ideles carry the restricted product topology.
proofSteps: The open subgroup U=∏_{v|∞}F_v××∏_{v finite}O_v× is R^(r₁+r₂)×K under archimedean logarithmic absolute values and polar decomposition, with K={±1}^r₁×(S¹)^r₂×∏O_v× compact Hausdorff abelian. GlobalNumberFields supplies the local-unit restricted-product topology; each finite O_v× is profinite and the product is compact.
Apply real-compact-open-character-extension. A character trivial on the principal subgroup descends to the Hausdorff idele-class quotient.

sources.locator: Lemma 12.5, pp. 210–211; Dikranjan’s extension results are expanded in the preceding nodes
sources.match: The idele instance is exactly the character-extension step of the isolating-twist proof. Its proof now reaches the pinned analytic baseline and current compact-group owner.

acceptance: For F=Q the archimedean compact factor is {±1}.
At a complex place use one real logarithmic factor and one circle.
The resulting character can have infinite order.

nodes.title: Topology of the isolation subgroup
nodes.statement: For F,S,v₀ and U_v^m as in isolating-twist-character, let A≤A_F× have component 1 outside S, arbitrary component at v₀ and component in U_v^m at the other v∈S. Multiplication F×_discrete×A→A_F× is a homeomorphism onto the closed subgroup F×A.
hypotheses: S consists of finite places, is finite and contains v₀; U_v^0=O_v×.
proofSteps: F×∩A={1}, since a principal idele equal to 1 outside S is 1. Multiplication is consequently injective.
For any 0<ε≤1, A_ε={a∈A:ε≤|a|≤ε⁻¹} is compact. All non-v₀ components lie in compact unit groups; the valuation at v₀ takes only finitely many possible values.

The product of a closed discrete subgroup with a compact subset is closed. On a neighbourhood whose norm lies in [ε,ε⁻¹], F×A coincides with F×A_ε, since the principal norm is 1. This proves closedness locally.

For a compact C⊂A_F×, its norm bounds place every possible a in a fixed compact A_ε. Then t∈C A_ε⁻¹∩F×, a finite set because principal ideles form a closed discrete subgroup. The preimage of C is therefore a closed subset of a finite set times A_ε and is compact. Multiplication is a continuous injective proper map between locally compact Hausdorff spaces, hence an embedding onto its already closed image. This proves the required product topology.

sources.locator: Lemma 12.5 proof, pp. 210–211
sources.match: The norm-bounded compact subsets establish both closedness and the product topology needed to define the character continuously.

acceptance: The arbitrary v₀ factor itself is not compact.
Principal ideles have norm 1, which is essential to the slab argument.
For m=0 every other local factor is O_v×.

nodes.title: Preliminary functional equation before local constants
nodes.statement: For finite-image complex ρ of G_F and a Hecke quasi-character ω, the product Λ(s,ρ⊗ω) of raw local L-factors continues meromorphically and satisfies Λ(s,ρ⊗ω)=E_pre(s,ρ,ω)Λ(1−s,ρ∨⊗ω⁻¹), where E_pre=A exp(Bs) with A≠0. The factor is multiplicative on virtual representations and E_pre,F(s,Ind_{G_K}^{G_F}σ,ω)=E_pre,K(s,σ,ω∘N_K/F). Its definition and proof use no higher-dimensional local epsilon factor.
hypotheses: F a number field; finite-image ρ; ω any continuous quasi-character, interpreted locally through geometric reciprocity; raw archimedean factors included.
proofSteps: Factor through a finite Galois group and use InductionRestriction Layer 6 Brauer induction, writing [ρ]=Σa_i Ind θ_i. Finite global reciprocity makes θ_i Hecke characters η_i over the corresponding fields K_i.
The projection formula and local L-induction identify Λ with ∏Λ_Ki(s,η_i(ω∘N))^a_i; handle archimedean induction with the imported real/complex factor formulas.

Multiply the one-dimensional Hecke functional equations. Their nonzero exponential factors give E_pre. It is independent of the Brauer expression because the ratio of the two nonzero meromorphic L-functions is intrinsic. Multiplicativity and global induction follow from these ratios and local L-inductivity. Real norm powers shift s and cause no new global carrier.

sources.match: Brauer induction gives meromorphy, the exponential functional-equation factor, additivity and global inductivity before §4 constructs local constants.

acceptance: For ρ=1 this is Hecke theory.
Negative Brauer coefficients require meromorphy, not holomorphy.
No local-epsilon-factor or final Artin product formula appears among the prerequisites.

nodes.title: Global product of local induction constants
nodes.statement: Let K/F be a finite separable extension of number fields, ψ nontrivial on A_F/F, ψ_K=ψ∘Tr_K/F, and choose local additive measures whose products are the respective Tamagawa measures. Put λ_v(K/F,ψ)=ε_Fv(⊕_{w|v}Ind_{W_Kw}^{W_Fv}1,ψ_v,dx_v)/∏_{w|v}ε_Kw(1,ψ_K,w,dy_w). For these Deligne constants, ∏_v λ_v=1. Accordingly the product of local constants is globally inductive for arbitrary finite-image representations with Hecke quasi-character twists. The individual λ_v need not be 1.
hypotheses: All places, including infinity; compatible trace characters and Tamagawa products; degree-zero local induction as in Deligne 4.1(3).
proofSteps: Subtract dim σ copies of the trivial representation before applying degree-zero local induction. Restoring them gives the displayed λ_v correction, raised to dim σ. Thus proving the product formula for these corrections suffices.

The outstanding calculation is ∏λ_v=1, not unrestricted local inductivity. Deligne 5.11 states the global product functional equation, but its proof paragraph invokes known arguments without giving this calculation. An identification of the induction correction with a scalar in a trace-pairing Fourier comparison has not been established in the sources read. Adelic Poisson alone does not justify it. This is the retained precise gap G2; the remaining steps below are conditional on that product formula.

Local additivity, Mackey restriction and the degree-zero axiom now prove global inductivity of ∏ε. Compare on the Brauer induction generators with the Hecke functional equation, hence with preliminary-artin-functional-equation. This identifies E_pre with ∏ε for every ρ and twist.

sources.locator: §3.11.3–3.11.4, p. 532; 4.1(3), p. 535; global construction 4.12, p. 544; 5.11 and its proof paragraph, p. 551
sources.match: Deligne states the product functional equation; the λ-product is its induction consequence. The source’s short proof does not discharge the explicit λ-product calculation in this revision; it remains G2.

acceptance: For K=F all λ_v are 1.
For a quadratic extension retain the local quadratic induction constants, including infinity.
Rescaling a single local measure changes λ_v; the product statement requires the Tamagawa product condition.

nodes.title: Finite splitting extensions for finite-dimensional algebras
nodes.statement: Every finite-dimensional algebra A over a field F admits a finite algebraic extension E/F such that every simple E⊗_F A-module is absolutely simple, equivalently its semisimple quotient is a finite product of full matrix algebras over E.
hypotheses: A finite-dimensional, unital, possibly noncommutative F-algebra. No restriction on char F.
proofSteps: Over an algebraic closure F̄, there are finitely many simple modules and their endomorphism rings are F̄. Import the Wedderburn/simple-block dictionary from SemisimpleAlgebras and finite-algebra radical infrastructure from QuiverRepresentations.
Choose bases in these simple modules. Their finitely many action matrices for an F-basis of A involve finitely many elements algebraic over F. They are contained in a finite extension E.

Combine all action maps into A_E→∏End_E(S_i). Its extension to F̄ is onto by the semisimple block dictionary, so a finite matrix-rank calculation proves it onto over E. The kernel extends to J(A_F̄), hence is nilpotent and lies in J(A_E). The split semisimple quotient has zero radical, giving the opposite inclusion. This identifies A_E/J as the product of full matrix blocks and exhausts its simples. The descended modules are absolutely simple by the full matrix-span criterion (R01.1/absolutely-irreducible, whose density proof works for an algebra action).

sources.locator: Theorem 9.2.6 and proof, p. 143; Proposition 9.2.5, p. 142
sources.match: Finite-dimensional algebras have a splitting field finite over the original field; the proof descends a finite list of simple-module matrices from an algebraic closure.

acceptance: For F=F_p, E is a finite field.
For A=M_n(F), E=F works.
This is not an entrywise descent theorem for an arbitrary representation displayed over a transcendental extension.

nodes.title: Simple modules of a split algebra after scalar extension
nodes.statement: Let A be a finite-dimensional F-algebra with A/J(A)≅∏_{i=1}^r M_ni(F). For any field extension K/F, J(K⊗A)=K⊗J(A) and (K⊗A)/J≅∏M_ni(K). Scalar extension gives a bijection of simple-module isomorphism classes, taking the i-th column module F^ni to K^ni. In particular every simple K⊗A-module descends up to isomorphism to F.
hypotheses: The split quotient hypothesis is explicit; K can be transcendental and need not be algebraically closed.
proofSteps: J(A) is nilpotent by the pinned Artinian theorem. Flatness of a field extension makes the scalar-extended quotient exact; the image K⊗J(A) remains nilpotent and is therefore contained in J(K⊗A).
The quotient is the indicated product of matrix algebras, hence semisimple and has zero radical. The radical upstairs maps to zero, proving the opposite inclusion.

A simple module is killed by the radical. Apply the imported Wedderburn simple-block dictionary: a matrix block has exactly its column module as a simple, and a product’s simples come from one block. The columns commute with scalar extension.

sources.locator: §9.2, splitting-field definition p. 142 and remarks p. 144; §9.8, Exercises 4 and 8(a), pp. 165–166; Artin–Wedderburn Theorem 2.1.3, pp. 15–16
sources.match: The split block description gives scalar-extension stability. The radical comparison here is proved under the split hypothesis and needs no general perfect-field radical theorem.

acceptance: A=M_n(F) has one simple of dimension n over every extension.
A=F[ε]/(ε²) retains its one-dimensional simple and nonzero radical.
Without the split hypothesis R→C for A=C gives two complex simples, so the hypothesis cannot be omitted.

nodes.title: Descent of characteristic-p simples up to conjugacy
nodes.statement: For any finite group Γ and algebraically closed field k of characteristic p, every irreducible r:Γ→GL_n(k) has a finite subfield k₀⊂k, an irreducible r₀:Γ→GL_n(k₀), and P∈GL_n(k) with r(g)=P r₀(g)P⁻¹. The field k₀ can be chosen splitting for every subgroup of Γ. The matrices of r themselves need not lie in a finite field.
hypotheses: Γ finite; k arbitrary algebraically closed of characteristic p; irreducible r.
proofSteps: Apply finite-algebra-splitting-field to the finite list of algebras F_pH for all subgroups H≤Γ and take their finite compositum. Embed this finite field k₀ in k.
Apply split-simple-scalar-extension to k₀Γ and k/k₀. The simple module of r is isomorphic to the scalar extension of a simple k₀Γ-module. Choose bases and write the isomorphism as P.

sources.locator: Theorem 9.2.6, p. 143; §9.2 remarks p. 144; §9.8, Exercises 4 and 8(a), pp. 165–166
sources.match: The finite splitting extension and split scalar-extension classification imply descent of simples for arbitrary algebraically closed coefficients.

acceptance: Conjugating a finite-field representation by a matrix with a transcendental entry is allowed.
For Γ a p-group the only simple is the trivial rank-one module.
The statement is about simple modules; it does not claim finite-field descent of all nonsemisimple modules.

nodes.title: Complete splitting modular systems exist
nodes.statement: For finite Γ and prime p there is a complete DVR R of mixed characteristic (0,p), with fraction field E a finite extension of Q_p and finite residue field k₀, such that E and k₀ split every subgroup of Γ and E contains roots of unity of the full exponent e of Γ. Reduction identifies prime-to-p roots with their residue roots. Compatible complex values of these roots define ordinary and Brauer characters.
hypotheses: Γ finite; prime p; complex root identification is algebraic, not a continuous embedding Q_p→C.
proofSteps: Choose a finite splitting field F_q for all subgroup algebras by finite-field-simple-descent. Take the unramified degree-f extension of Q_p with residue F_q, and then a finite compositum with Q_p(ζ_e). Its ring of integers is a complete DVR, its residue extends F_q and hence remains splitting by split-simple-scalar-extension.

The characteristic-zero cyclotomic splitting theorem in InductionRestriction Layer 6 makes E splitting for all subgroups. Reduction on μ_m, p∤m, is injective because m is a unit and surjective because all m roots remain distinct; these roots are integral units.
Choose an embedding of Q(ζ_e) in C; the values of finite-group characters lie in that field, so no topological embedding of the complete field is required.

sources.locator: §9.4, definition and existence of p-modular systems, pp. 148–149; Lemma 10.1.1, p. 170
sources.match: Splitting modular systems are obtained by finite extensions and may be complete; only prime-to-p roots survive reduction.

acceptance: If p divides e, primitive e-th roots are required upstairs, not in k₀.
For Γ={1}, Z_p suffices.
Completeness is imposed for lifting projectives, and is not imposed on the number-field localisation in the end target.

nodes.title: Projectives lift over a complete DVR
nodes.statement: Let R be a complete DVR with residue field k₀ and Γ finite. Every finitely generated projective k₀Γ-module P is the reduction of a projective RΓ-lattice P̂, unique up to isomorphism among RΓ-lattice lifts. For projective P̂,Q̂, Hom_RΓ(P̂,Q̂) is finite free over R and its reduction is Hom_k₀Γ(P,Q). The same Hom base-change holds with any RΓ-lattice as target.
hypotheses: R complete; finite Γ; finite-rank free R-module targets; projectivity is over the group algebra.
proofSteps: Write P as the image of an idempotent in a matrix algebra over k₀Γ using the existing finite-algebra projective infrastructure. Lift the idempotent successively modulo πⁿ: at each step the kernel is square-zero. The polynomial correction to an almost-idempotent yields a lift; completeness gives the limiting idempotent and its image P̂.

For any lattice lift L, lift P̂→L of the residual isomorphism using projectivity. Nakayama gives surjectivity and equal R-ranks imply isomorphism. This proves uniqueness and that every lattice lift is projective.

Hom out of a projective summand is the corresponding idempotent summand of Hom from a finite free RΓ-module. As an R-module it is finite free, and taking that summand commutes with reduction. Orthogonal primitive idempotents and covers themselves are imported from QuiverRepresentations Layer 3; their complete-DVR lifts are the new content.

sources.locator: Propositions 9.4.3 and 9.4.5, pp. 149–152; projective Hom comparison in the proof of Proposition 10.2.1, p. 175
sources.match: Completeness lifts idempotents and projectives; projective Hom reduction is an idempotent-summand argument.

acceptance: The regular module lifts to RΓ.
A lift of a projective cover need not have irreducible characteristic-zero generic fibre.
The assertion is not made over Z or a noncomplete DVR.

nodes.title: Projective characters vanish on p-singular elements
nodes.statement: For a splitting p-modular system with R complete and a projective RΓ-lattice P̂, its ordinary character χ vanishes at every g whose order is divisible by p. Moreover the order of a Sylow p-subgroup divides χ(1).
hypotheses: Finite Γ; χ valued through compatible cyclotomic roots; projectivity over RΓ.
proofSteps: Restriction to a subgroup preserves projectivity since RΓ is free over its subgroup algebra. For a Sylow p-subgroup, projectives over k₀P are free: the augmentation ideal is nilpotent and the group algebra is local. The unique projective lift is free over RP, yielding the dimension divisibility.

For g write ⟨g⟩=⟨s⟩×⟨t⟩ with s prime-to-p and t a nontrivial p-element. The modular indecomposable projectives are S⊗k₀⟨t⟩. The prime-to-p simple S lifts to an R⟨s⟩ projective by averaging, and induction gives its R⟨g⟩ lift.

By projective-modular-lift uniqueness all projective summands have this form. The induced-character formula is zero at g, since no conjugate of g lies in ⟨s⟩. Add the summands. The local p-group assertion follows by induction on its order using a central order-p element and its nilpotent (z−1) ideal.

sources.locator: Theorem 8.1.1, Lemma 8.1.2 and Corollary 8.1.3, pp. 120–121; Lemma 9.6.2, pp. 163–164
sources.match: A projective’s degree has the Sylow divisibility and its character is zero whenever the element’s order is divisible by p.

acceptance: For a nontrivial p-group the regular character is zero off 1.
The trivial module of a p-group is not projective.
p-singular here means order divisible by p, not only order a power of p.

nodes.title: Hom dimension as a projective Brauer pairing
nodes.statement: For finite Γ, a splitting field k₀ of characteristic p, a finitely generated projective k₀Γ-module P and a finite-dimensional k₀Γ-module U, dim_k₀ Hom_k₀Γ(P,U)=|Γ|⁻¹Σ_{g p-regular}φ_P(g⁻¹)φ_U(g), for compatible Brauer characters. The same formula holds over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p.
hypotheses: P projective; U arbitrary, not assumed to lift or be semisimple. Choose a complete splitting system and compatible τ for the finite-field case.
proofSteps: P⊗U∨ with diagonal action is projective: tensor a free k₀Γ-module with U∨ and untwist the action on the second tensor factor to exhibit a free module; pass to summands. Current Tau Ceti already exposes the Hom formulation as Representation.instProjectiveAsModuleLinHom in RepresentationTheory/LinHom.lean; consume it when porting instead of replanning this helper. This current-library observation is not a pinned-baseline citation.

Lift this projective module to Q̂. Projective-modular-lift with target the trivial lattice R shows dim Hom_k₀Γ(P⊗U∨,k₀)=rank Hom_RΓ(Q̂,R). The ordinary characteristic-zero character inner product computes that rank.

projective-character-vanishing deletes the p-singular terms. On p-regular elements the ordinary character of Q̂ is φ_P(g)φ_U(g⁻¹), by the root reduction and tensor/dual Brauer API. Replace g by g⁻¹ and use Hom(P⊗U∨,k₀)≅Hom(P,U).

For arbitrary algebraically closed k, projectives and simples are obtained by scalar extension from a finite splitting field. The formula is additive in U, by exactness of Hom(P,−) and the Brauer short-exact-sequence API. A composition series therefore reduces the calculation to simple U; use split-simple-scalar-extension and Hom base change. No arbitrary-k lift of U is asserted.

sources.locator: Proposition 8.1.4, pp. 121–122; Proposition 10.2.1 and proof, pp. 174–175
sources.match: The projective tensor-dual lifts even when U does not; characteristic-zero averaging and p-singular vanishing give the Hom formula.

acceptance: For P=k₀Γ, the sum is dim U.
For P a projective cover and U simple the result is δ after invoking the separate split Hom contract.
Without projectivity the formula is not asserted.

nodes.title: Brauer’s p-regular class-count theorem
nodes.statement: For a finite group Γ and a splitting field k of characteristic p, the number of isomorphism classes of simple kΓ-modules equals the number of p-regular conjugacy classes.
hypotheses: Finite Γ; split kΓ; no p-solvability or Maschke hypothesis.
proofSteps: Let A=kΓ, S the vector span of commutators ab−ba, and T={a:a^(pⁿ)∈S for some n}. Modulo S, taking p-th powers is additive and Frobenius-semilinear, so T is a vector subspace. S is not treated as an ideal.

The nilpotent radical J lies in T. Powering again kills a possible error in J, so T/J is exactly the analogous subspace in A/J. In each split matrix block, trace(a^(pⁿ))=trace(a)^(pⁿ), hence that subspace is the trace-zero hyperplane. Thus codim T is the number of simple blocks.

For g=st, with s p-regular and t of p-power order commuting with s, (g−s)^(pⁿ)=0 for sufficiently large n. Thus p-regular conjugacy representatives span A/T. For independence choose n sufficiently large, with pⁿ≡1 modulo the prime-to-p exponent; a relation powered into S has the same class representatives with nonzero coefficients raised to pⁿ. The description of S by zero coefficient-sum on each conjugacy class rules it out. Consequently codim T is the number of p-regular classes.

sources.locator: Lemmas 9.3.1–9.3.5 and Theorem 9.3.6, pp. 145–147
sources.match: A commutator-span and p-power calculation equates the split semisimple block count with the p-regular class count.

acceptance: A p-group has one simple and one p-regular class.
If p∤|Γ| all classes are p-regular.
For S₃ at p=2 there are two such classes, hence two simples.

nodes.title: p-rational characters
nodes.statement: For finite Γ and prime p, put r=|Γ|/p^{v_p(|Γ|)}. Define IsPRational(p,χ) by χ(g)∈Q(μ_r)⊂C for every g∈Γ. For ordinary characters, whose values already lie in Q(μ_|Γ|), this agrees with Isaacs’s condition that all values lie in some cyclotomic field of conductor prime to p. It is equivalently invariance under Gal(Q(μ_|Γ|)/Q(μ_r)). The light predicate is defined for any function Γ→C; the equivalences involving ordinary characters require that input.
hypotheses: Γ finite; p prime; χ an ordinary character for the cyclotomic/Galois compatibility assertion.
proofSteps: Use the prime-to-p complement of |Γ| and the intermediate field generated by its complex roots of unity to define the value-membership predicate.

Ordinary character values lie in Q(μ_|Γ|) by finite-order eigenvalues. The cyclotomic fixed-field description gives the Galois characterisation; intersection with a field of prime-to-p conductor removes the p-power cyclotomic part. This exact character-field adapter is requested from InductionRestriction Part II.

sources.locator: Definition 1.1, p. 171; cyclotomic Galois notation in §4, p. 177
sources.match: p-rational ordinary characters have values in a cyclotomic field of conductor prime to p. The fixed-field formulation is the one used by the extension and uniqueness proofs.

uses.how: Galois invariance and uniqueness preserve the p-rational lift.
The odd-p cyclotomic action selects the unique p-rational constituent.
The induction constructs a p-rational ordinary lift for every prime.
Odd-p uniqueness compares p-rational lifts, including their normal-subgroup constituents.

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.isPRational
api.statement: The predicate on functions Γ→C given by value membership in Q(μ_r), with r the prime-to-p part of |Γ|.

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.isPRational_iff_forall_mem
api.statement: IsPRational(p,χ) iff every χ(g) belongs to the indicated intermediate field; no irreducibility is required.

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.isPRational_iff_galois_fixed
api.statement: For an ordinary character, IsPRational iff every automorphism of Q(μ_|Γ|) fixing Q(μ_r) fixes every character value. The ordinary-character cyclotomic-value hypothesis is required.

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.isPRational_precomp_mulAut
api.statement: Precomposing χ with an automorphism of Γ preserves and reflects IsPRational.

tests.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.isPRational_trivial_test
tests.statement: The constant rank-one trivial character is p-rational for every finite group and every prime.

tests.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.isPRational_sign_two_test
tests.statement: At p=2 both ordinary characters of C₂, including the sign character, are 2-rational: their values are rational. Thus p-rationality alone does not give unique lifts at p=2.

tests.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.isPRational_odd_prime_test
tests.statement: For odd p a nontrivial linear character of C_p is not p-rational: its primitive p-th root value is not rational, whereas r=1.

tests.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.isPRational_coprime_cyclic_test
tests.statement: If ℓ is prime and ℓ≠p, every linear character of C_ℓ is p-rational, since r=ℓ and all values are ℓ-th roots.

acceptance: The two C₂ characters are both admitted at p=2.
At odd p only the trivial linear character of C_p is admitted.

nodes.title: Modular Clifford correspondence
nodes.statement: Let N◁Γ be finite and k algebraically closed of arbitrary characteristic. If S is simple over kN and T its inertia group, induction gives a bijection from simple kT-modules whose N-restriction is S-isotypic to simple kΓ-modules whose N-restriction contains S. Restriction of a simple Γ-module to N is semisimple with equally repeated conjugate simples, and the T-module is its S-isotypic component.
hypotheses: N normal; simple modules finite-dimensional; characteristic may divide |Γ|.
proofSteps: The N-socle of a simple Γ-module is nonzero and Γ-stable, so equals the whole module. Its isotypic summands are permuted transitively, with equal multiplicities; this restriction statement is already R01.1/clifford-isotypic-decomposition.
The S-isotypic component is T-stable. Translating it along Γ/T gives the direct sum of distinct isotypic components and identifies its induction with the original module.

Conversely restrict an induced S-isotypic T-simple to N: any Γ-submodule is a semisimple N-submodule and its isotypic components intersect the original T-summand. If nonzero, transitivity and T-simplicity force all summands. The two constructions are inverse. No average over Γ or Maschke argument is used.

sources.locator: Lemma 5.1, pp. 178–179; §2 Clifford restriction usage, p. 173
sources.match: The Brauer inertia correspondence is the module-theoretic Clifford correspondence without a semisimplicity hypothesis on kΓ.

acceptance: For N={1}, T=Γ and the correspondence is the identity.
For N=Γ it is the identity on its chosen simple.
The hypothesis p∤|Γ| is absent.

nodes.title: Lifting correspondence at prime-to-p index
nodes.statement: Let N◁Γ with p∤[Γ:N]. Let θ be an irreducible ordinary character of N, with θ*=μ an irreducible Brauer character, and suppose μ^g=μ implies θ^g=θ. Then χ↦χ* is a bijection between ordinary irreducibles lying over θ and Brauer irreducibles lying over μ. If θ is p-rational, all those χ are p-rational.
hypotheses: θ* denotes restriction to p-regular elements with fixed compatible root identification; inertia equality is required.
proofSteps: Induction of a simple N-module is semisimple at prime-to-p index: an N-equivariant splitting can be averaged over Γ/N and divided by its invertible order. This yields Frobenius reciprocity for the constituent multiplicities (Isaacs 2.2).

Expand θ^Γ and μ^Γ into constituents, using ordinary and modular Clifford equal multiplicities. Nonnegative decomposition numbers dχφ give bφ=Σχ aχdχφ and aχ=Σφ dχφbφ. Substitution forces each row to have exactly one nonzero entry equal to 1, with disjoint supports; all constituents over μ occur. Brauer independence used here is brauer-character-recognition.
If θ is p-rational, a Galois automorphism fixing the prime-to-p cyclotomic field leaves θ and every Brauer restriction fixed. Uniqueness in this bijection forces each χ to be fixed.

sources.locator: Theorem 2.2, pp. 173–174; Theorem 3.1 and proof, pp. 174–175; Corollary 5.2, p. 179
sources.match: Prime-to-p index and equality of inertia groups give the ordinary/Brauer bijection and the p-rational consequence.

acceptance: When N=Γ it returns θ and μ.
Dropping inertia equality is not allowed.
This is not the usual characteristic-zero Frobenius inner product for arbitrary modular induction.

nodes.title: Lift comparison across a p-group quotient
nodes.statement: Let N◁Γ with Γ/N a p-group, θ∈Irr(N), T its inertia group, and η∈Irr(T) an extension of θ. Assume θ*=μ∈IBr(N) and μ^g=μ implies g∈T. Then (Ind_T^Γη)* is the unique irreducible Brauer character of Γ lying over μ.
hypotheses: The quotient is a p-group, not just an index divisible by p; extendibility to T is an explicit hypothesis.
proofSteps: Ordinary Clifford identifies the induced ordinary irreducible and its restriction as the sum of distinct conjugates of θ. Modular Clifford gives restriction of any simple over μ as e times the same sum of conjugates of μ.
Every p-regular element of Γ lies in N, because its image in the p-group quotient is trivial. Thus the full Brauer character equals e times the restriction of the induced ordinary character.
The latter is itself a nonzero nonnegative integral combination of simple Brauer characters (reduce a stable lattice). Comparing multiplicities with a single simple forces e=1 and proves uniqueness.

sources.locator: Lemma 4.1 and proof, pp. 175–176
sources.match: The p-group quotient places all p-regular elements in N and forces the induced lift’s restriction to be the single desired Brauer character.

acceptance: For N=Γ the comparison is immediate.
For quotient C_p all p-regular elements are in N.
Existence of the extension η is proved by the next targets, not assumed automatically.

nodes.title: Gallagher’s determinant-order extension
nodes.statement: If N◁Γ, Γ/N is a p-group and θ∈Irr(N) is Γ-invariant with p∤θ(1) and p∤o(θ), then θ has a unique extension χ∈Irr(Γ) with p∤o(χ). Here o is the order of the determinant character. If θ is p-rational, so is χ.
hypotheses: Finite Γ; invariant θ; both degree and determinant order prime to p. No odd-p hypothesis.
proofSteps: For index p, ordinary cyclic-quotient extension is an exact InductionRestriction Part II input: for an invariant irreducible of N and cyclic Γ/N, choose an intertwiner for a generator and rescale its central scalar using a root in C; this makes its power agree with the N-action. Let η be an extension and m=o(θ). The p-part of det η is killed by twisting η by a suitable power of (det η)^m, which factors through Γ/N. Choose b with θ(1)mb≡−1 mod p.
Any other extension is η times a linear character of the p-quotient; since its degree is prime to p, a nontrivial twist gives determinant with nontrivial p-part. This proves uniqueness.

For a larger p-quotient choose a central order-p subgroup, extend to its preimage and use uniqueness to retain Γ-invariance; induct on the quotient. Galois conjugation preserves determinant order, so uniqueness also proves p-rationality.

sources.locator: Theorem 4.2, p. 176; Corollary 4.7, p. 178
sources.match: The determinant normalization supplies the extension used in the all-prime strengthened induction.

acceptance: For θ=1 the normalized extension is 1.
For p=2 the theorem still applies.
A nontrivial linear twist of a p-quotient violates the determinant-order normalization.

nodes.title: Unique p-rational constituents over p-group quotients
nodes.statement: For odd p, N◁Γ with Γ/N a p-group and p-rational θ∈Irr(N), Ind_N^Γθ has exactly one p-rational irreducible constituent χ. If θ*=μ is irreducible and μ^g=μ implies θ^g=θ, then χ* is the unique irreducible Brauer character of Γ over μ. In particular an invariant θ has a unique p-rational extension.
hypotheses: p odd; p-rational means values lie in Q(ζ_r), where r is the prime-to-p part of |Γ|; equivalently fixed by Gal(Q(ζ_|Γ|)/Q(ζ_r)).
proofSteps: In the invariant index-p case take an ordinary extension η. A generator σ of the p-power cyclotomic Galois group satisfies η^σ=λη for a quotient linear character λ. At odd p its action on μ_p is nontrivial. A power of λ therefore twists η to a σ-fixed extension. The same nontrivial action makes it unique.

Induct through a central order-p subgroup of Γ/N. In the general non-invariant case pass to the ordinary inertia group and use ordinary Clifford correspondence. Induction preserves p-rationality; for the converse in the correspondence both θ and the induced character are fixed by σ, so uniqueness of the inertia correspondent fixes it too.

Under the Brauer hypotheses apply p-group-index-lift-comparison. This target, together with the prime-to-p-index correspondence, supplies the restriction/uniqueness induction in Isaacs §6, not merely existence.

sources.locator: Theorem 4.3, pp. 177–178; Lemma 4.4 and Theorem 4.5, p. 178
sources.match: Odd p allows the unique p-rational extension and unique p-rational constituent, with the Brauer comparison under its inertia hypotheses.

acceptance: At p=2 and Γ=C₂, both ordinary linear characters are 2-rational and reduce to the same Brauer character; uniqueness fails.
N=Γ returns θ.
No prime-to-p degree assumption is made in this odd-p target.

nodes.title: Automorphism-equivariant strengthened Fong–Swan theorem
nodes.statement: For finite p-solvable Γ and φ∈IBr(Γ), there is a p-rational χ∈Irr(Γ) with χ*=φ and χ^a=χ for every a∈Aut(Γ) with φ^a=φ. If p divides φ(1), there exists a characteristic subgroup N of Γ for which the number of distinct simple constituents of φ_N is divisible by p.
hypotheses: All primes p, including 2; p-solvable means a normal series with p-group or prime-to-p factors; χ and φ use compatible τ. The degree assertion is an implication, not its converse.
proofSteps: Induct simultaneously on the full stated assertion. If a characteristic N has a p-divisible number of constituents, modular Clifford passes to its proper inertia group. Induct there and induce the ordinary lift. An automorphism fixing φ permutes its N-constituents; compose it with an inner conjugation to fix the chosen constituent and inertia correspondent. The induction hypothesis then fixes the induced lift.

Otherwise every proper characteristic M has constituents μ of prime-to-p degree, by the strengthened inductive degree clause. Their chosen lifts θ are p-rational, equivariant, and have prime-to-p degree; the number of conjugates is prime to p.

If O^p(Γ)<Γ, use M=O^p(Γ). Its p-group quotient and the prime-to-p orbit make θ invariant. Since O^p(M)=M, M has no nontrivial p-group quotient; its determinant character has prime-to-p order. Apply determinant-order-extension and p-group-index-lift-comparison. Uniqueness gives equivariance and p-rationality.

Otherwise O^{p′}(Γ)<Γ by p-solvability. Use the coprime-index-lift-correspondence and its p-rational consequence. Its uniqueness gives equivariance after adjusting by conjugation. The ordinary Clifford relative-degree divisibility χ(1)/θ(1) | [Γ:M] gives prime-to-p degree; this ordinary theorem is an explicit InductionRestriction Part II request. Thus in this second case p∤φ(1), completing the degree implication.

sources.locator: Theorem 5.4 and full proof, pp. 179–180
sources.match: The induction preserves an automorphism stabilizer and the characteristic-subgroup degree alternative; these are necessary for its second case.

acceptance: For a p-group φ=1 and χ=1 works even at p=2.
If p divides the Brauer degree, the characteristic-subgroup clause must be retained.
Equivariance requires the characteristic, rather than merely normal, choice of subgroup.

nodes.title: Stability of GL₂ factors under highly ramified twists
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic zero, ψ a nontrivial additive character of F, and π an irreducible admissible representation of GL₂(F) with central character ω_π. For a quasi-character χ of F^× write c(χ) for its conductor exponent. (i) There is an integer m(π) such that L(s, χ⊗π) = L(s, χ⁻¹⊗π̃) = 1 whenever c(χ) > m(π). (ii) If π₁ and π₂ are irreducible admissible representations with the same central character, there is an integer m such that ε(s, χ⊗π₁, ψ) = ε(s, χ⊗π₂, ψ) whenever c(χ) > m; with (i) this gives γ(s, χ⊗π₁, ψ) = γ(s, χ⊗π₂, ψ) for such χ, where γ(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ)L(1−s, χ⁻¹⊗π̃)/L(s, χ⊗π). (iii) More precisely, for any factorisation ω_π = μ₁μ₂ into quasi-characters, ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = ε(s, χμ₁, ψ)ε(s, χμ₂, ψ) once c(χ) is large compared with π, c(μ₁) and c(μ₂); the right side is a product of Tate's GL₁ constants and depends on π only through ω_π. The bound m depends on π₁, π₂ and ψ, not on χ.
hypotheses: F is a finite extension of Q_p; ψ: F → C^× is a nontrivial continuous additive character.
π, π₁, π₂ are irreducible admissible representations of GL₂(F); in (ii) ω_{π₁} = ω_{π₂}.
The local factors L, ε and γ are those of Jacquet–Langlands §2–§3 (equivalently Godement–Jacquet for n = 2), in the normalisation fixed by R16.3.
c(χ) is the conductor exponent of AL.1/local-quasicharacter-conductor; 'sufficiently ramified' means c(χ) larger than an explicit bound depending on π (and on ψ through its conductor).
proofSteps: One-dimensional and principal-series representations: L(s, χ⊗π(μ₁, μ₂)) = L(s, χμ₁)L(s, χμ₂) and ε(s, χ⊗π(μ₁, μ₂), ψ) = ε(s, χμ₁, ψ)ε(s, χμ₂, ψ) (R16.3/principal-series-parameter and the Jacquet–Langlands product formula); once c(χ) exceeds c(μ₁) and c(μ₂), both χμᵢ are ramified, so the L-factors are 1 (AL.1/ramified-local-theory) and the ε-factor is the stated product. Twists of Steinberg are constituents of a reducible principal series and have the same twisted factors as it for highly ramified χ (JL70 p. 58, reduction step).

Supercuspidal π: L(s, χ⊗π) = 1 for every χ (R16.2/local-classification and R16.3/supercuspidal-parameter). For the ε-factor, JL70 compute ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ) through the Kirillov model (R16.2/supercuspidal-kirillov): for c(χ) large the Mellin transform of a vector supported near 1 only sees the central character, which yields the product ε(s, χμ₁, ψ)ε(s, χμ₂, ψ) for any μ₁μ₂ = ω_π (JL70 Proposition 3.8, proof).
(ii) follows from (iii) applied to π₁ and π₂ with the same factorisation of the common central character, and (i).
acceptance: For π = π(μ₁, μ₂) a ramified principal series and χ with c(χ) > max(c(μ₁), c(μ₂)), the twisted L-factor is 1 and ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ) is the product of the two Tate constants.

Two supercuspidal representations with the same central character have equal twisted γ-factors for all sufficiently ramified χ, although they need not be isomorphic: stability alone never distinguishes them (non-example for using stability as a converse theorem).

The hypothesis on central characters is necessary in (ii): for π an unramified principal series and η an unramified character with η² ≠ 1, the highly ramified ε-factors of χ⊗(π⊗η) and χ⊗π differ by the factor η²(ϖ)^{c(χ)+n(ψ)} (n(ψ) the conductor exponent of ψ), which is not 1 for suitable large c(χ).

sources.locator: §3, Proposition 3.8 (i)–(iii), printed pp. 57–58 (PDF pp. 63–64 of the IAS edition)
sources.match: Jacquet–Langlands prove that for every irreducible π the twisted L-factors are 1 once the order of χ is large, that two representations with the same central character have equal twisted ε-factors for such χ, and the product formula for ε in terms of any factorisation of the central character; the statement here is theirs in the γ-factor form used by the isolation argument.

sources.locator: §12, proof of Theorem 12.2, printed p. 211 (PDF p. 217)
sources.match: The isolation argument invokes Proposition 3.8 exactly in this way: at the auxiliary places the highly ramified twist makes the L-factors trivial and the ε-factor depend only on the central character.

nodes.title: The GL₂ local converse theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic zero and ψ a nontrivial additive character. Let π and π′ be irreducible infinite-dimensional admissible representations of GL₂(F) with the same central character. Then π ≅ π′ if and only if γ(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = γ(s, χ⊗π′, ψ) for every quasi-character χ of F^×. Equivalently, without the central-character hypothesis, π ≅ π′ as soon as L(s, χ⊗π) = L(s, χ⊗π′) and ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = ε(s, χ⊗π′, ψ) for every character χ of F^× (Bushnell–Henniart's form, which also covers one-dimensional representations). It suffices to test χ of finite order with χ(ϖ) = 1 for a fixed uniformiser ϖ: every quasi-character is such a χ times |·|^t, and twisting by |·|^t replaces s by s + t in all three factors.
hypotheses: F is a finite extension of Q_p, ψ a nontrivial additive character, ϖ a uniformiser.
π, π′ are irreducible admissible infinite-dimensional (equivalently generic, R16.2/local-classification) representations of GL₂(F) with ω_π = ω_{π′}.
γ(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ)L(1−s, χ⁻¹⊗π̃)/L(s, χ⊗π) with the Jacquet–Langlands factors.
proofSteps: The implication from isomorphism to equality of factors is immediate.

Converse (JL70 Theorem 2.18 and Corollary 2.19): in the Kirillov model both representations are realised on spaces containing C_c^∞(F^×); the local functional equation of Theorem 2.18(iv) expresses the action of the Weyl element on C_c^∞(F^×) through the twisted γ-factors, by Mellin inversion over the characters of O_F^× and the variable s. Equal γ-factors and equal central characters therefore give the same action of the Borel subgroup and of the Weyl element on the common subspace, which generates; so π ≅ π′.

Reduction to finite-order twists with χ(ϖ) = 1: a quasi-character χ equals χ₀|·|^t with χ₀(ϖ) = 1 and χ₀ of finite order on O_F^× (it is continuous on a profinite group), and γ(s, χ₀|·|^t⊗π, ψ) = γ(s + t, χ₀⊗π, ψ).

Bushnell–Henniart prove the version with L and ε (27.1): by 27.2 a representation is cuspidal exactly when all its twisted L-factors are 1, so equal twisted factors separate cuspidal from non-cuspidal representations; non-cuspidal ones are then recovered from their principal-series parameters, and cuspidal ones from their types through Gauss sums (27.8).
acceptance: For π = π(μ₁, μ₂) and π′ = π(μ₁′, μ₂′) irreducible principal series with equal central characters, equal twisted γ-factors force {μ₁, μ₂} = {μ₁′, μ₂′}: twist by χ = μ₁⁻¹ and compare the zero of 1/L(s, χ⊗π) at s = 0.

For η the unramified quadratic character, π and π⊗η have the same central character and γ(s, χ⊗π⊗η, ψ) = γ(s + πi/log q, χ⊗π, ψ); the criterion says π ≅ π⊗η exactly when every twisted γ-factor is invariant under this shift of s, which holds for the supercuspidal representations induced from the unramified quadratic extension and fails for unramified principal series π(μ, ν) with {μη, νη} ≠ {μ, ν}.
A one-dimensional representation χ∘det is excluded from the γ-form (not generic), but is covered by Bushnell–Henniart's L-and-ε form.

nodes.title: A global twist with one prescribed component and high ramification elsewhere
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, S a finite set of finite places, v₀ ∈ S, χ₀ a quasi-character of F_{v₀}^×, and (m_v)_{v ∈ S∖{v₀}} nonnegative integers. There is a quasi-character ω of the idele class group C_F = F^×\A_F^× whose component at v₀ is χ₀ and whose component ω_v at each v ∈ S∖{v₀} is nontrivial on U_v^{m_v}, where U_v^0 = O_v^× and U_v^m = 1 + 𝔭_v^m for m ≥ 1, so that c(ω_v) > m_v. Nothing is imposed at the other places; ω has finite order on the units at every finite place but need not have finite order globally. This is Jacquet–Langlands's Lemma 12.5, which is the only global character input of the all-place upgrade; the finite-order prescription at several places (Chevalley's congruence theorem) is not needed for it.
hypotheses: F is a number field; S is a finite set of finite places; v₀ ∈ S.
χ₀: F_{v₀}^× → C^× is a continuous quasi-character; m_v ≥ 0 are integers for v ∈ S∖{v₀}.
c(χ) is the least m ≥ 0 such that χ is trivial on U_v^m, with U_v^0 = O_v^× and U_v^m = 1 + 𝔭_v^m for m ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Reduce to a unitary χ₀: write χ₀ = |·|^r χ₀′ with χ₀′ unitary and multiply the character obtained for χ₀′ by |·|_A^r.
Use isolation-subgroup-topology to identify F×A with the closed topological product F×_discrete×A. The compact norm slabs A_ε control the inverse as well as closedness.

Choose a continuous unitary character of A equal to the unitary χ₀ at v₀ and nontrivial on each U_v^{m_v} at the other places. The latter compact groups have nontrivial finite quotients. Extend by 1 on F^×, using isolation-subgroup-topology, then extend this character from the closed subgroup F^×A to the idele group by idele-character-extension. The exact idele instance is proved through the real/compact/open extension targets, with CompactGroups supplying Peter–Weyl; GlobalNumberFields Layer 9 is not assigned an unstated extension theorem. The resulting character descends to C_F (JL70 p. 211). For the strict conductor bound in this statement one can also apply the printed Lemma 12.5 with bounds m_v+1.
acceptance: With S = {v₀} the lemma only asks for a Hecke character with prescribed component at one place.

For F = Q, S = {p} and χ₀ unramified with χ₀(p) = −1, the unitary unramified character ω = |·|_A^{iπ/log p} is admissible; it has infinite order, so the lemma is not a statement about finite-order characters.
For m_v = 0, nontriviality is on O_v^×; the set 1 + O_v is not used as a multiplicative subgroup. In the Lean witness, require both valuation(u)=1 and valuation(u−1)≤q_v^(-m_v).

sources.match: Jacquet and Langlands construct a quasi-character of C_F with prescribed component at one place of S and conductor exponent greater than m_v at each of the others, by extending a character from the closed subgroup F^×A.

nodes.title: Functional equation of twisted Artin L-functions
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, ψ = ⊗ψ_v a nontrivial character of A_F/F, and dx = ∏dx_v the Tamagawa measure. Let ρ: G_F → GL_n(C) be continuous with finite image and ω a continuous quasi-character of C_F. At each place put V_v = ρ|_{W_{F_v}} ⊗ (ω_v ∘ Art_v⁻¹), where Art_v sends a uniformiser to geometric Frobenius and its inverse is read on the abelianisation. Define Λ(s,ρ⊗ω) by the product of these local L-factors, including the archimedean Γ-factors. It converges in a right half-plane, continues meromorphically, and satisfies Λ(s,ρ⊗ω) = ε(s,ρ⊗ω) Λ(1−s,ρ∨⊗ω⁻¹), with ε(s,ρ⊗ω) = ∏_v ε(s,V_v,ψ_v,dx_v). Almost all local constants equal 1, and the product is independent of the choice of ψ on A_F/F. No holomorphy is asserted. The notation ρ⊗ω denotes this compatible family of local twists, without requiring a global Weil group.
hypotheses: F is a number field; ρ: G_F → GL_n(C) is a continuous homomorphism; ω: A_F^×/F^× → C^× is a continuous quasi-character.

Local reciprocity uses geometric Frobenius. For each finite Galois extension K/F, finite global Artin reciprocity turns a finite Galois character of G_K into a finite-order Hecke character compatibly with the local maps and norms; invert the arithmetic Artin map if necessary.
Local constants: Deligne's ε(V_v, ψ_v, dx_v) at finite places (R01.2/local-epsilon-factor) and the archimedean constants of AL.1 and R16.3/archimedean-factor-comparison.
proofSteps: ρ factors through G = Gal(L/F) for a finite Galois L/F (R01.1/finite-galois-factorisation). By Brauer's induction theorem (Tau Ceti InductionRestriction, Layer 6) the character of ρ is an integral combination Σ nᵢ Ind_{Hᵢ}^{G} θᵢ of characters induced from linear characters θᵢ of subgroups Hᵢ = Gal(L/Kᵢ).

For each θᵢ use finite global Artin reciprocity to obtain a finite-order Hecke character ηᵢ of C_{Kᵢ}, with the geometric convention. Twist ηᵢ by ω∘N_{Kᵢ/F}. The projection formula for finite-group induction, followed by local restriction and reciprocity, identifies the associated local virtual representations with the local twists of ρ. No induction between global Weil groups is used.

preliminary-artin-functional-equation gives meromorphy and the nonzero exponential functional-equation factor by Brauer and Hecke theory, independently of local epsilon existence. The finite Galois and norm-twist dictionaries use no global Weil group.

Use R01.2/local-epsilon-factor only after its global input is retargeted to preliminary-artin-functional-equation. Conditional on the recorded G2 product proof, global-induction-constant-product supplies the λ correction and identifies E_pre with the product of local constants via Brauer induction. Determinant and norm product formulas prove independence under ψ↦ψ(a·), a∈F×. The conductor-normalized automorphic completion is converted to raw local factors before cancellation.
acceptance: For ρ trivial of dimension one the statement is Hecke–Tate's functional equation for Λ(s, ω).

For ρ = Ind_{G_K}^{G_F}1 and ω = 1 the completed function is the completed Dedekind zeta function of K, with poles at 0 and 1. Thus meromorphy cannot be strengthened to holomorphy. For a norm-power twist |·|^t these poles shift to −t and 1−t; arbitrary quasi-characters are not restricted to imaginary norm powers.
For a two-dimensional dihedral ρ = Ind θ the equation coincides with that of the Hecke L-function of θ·(ω∘N), consistent with JL70 Proposition 12.1.

sources.locator: §3.12(A)–(C), printed p. 533 (PDF p. 33)
sources.match: Finite-image representations twisted by quasi-characters have continuation and a preliminary functional equation via Brauer induction and the one-dimensional case, before the local-constant theorem. This separates the global input used in local existence from the final product formula.

sources.match: Existence and uniqueness of local constants that are multiplicative in exact sequences, scale with the measure, are inductive in degree zero and equal Tate's constants for characters.

For a representation of the global Weil group, the global L-function and the product of local constants satisfy the functional equation; Deligne derives it from the preceding local results and the classical arguments (Brauer induction, Hecke).

nodes.title: From weak Artin matching to matching at every place
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) continuous, restricted locally to W_{F_v}, and π a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL₂(A_F). For each place v let π(ρ_v) be the irreducible generic representation of GL₂(F_v) whose unitary R16.3 parameter rec (geometric reciprocity) (AF.1 at archimedean v) is ρ|_{W_{F_v}}. Suppose there is a finite set T of finite places such that π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for every finite v ∉ T and for every archimedean v. Then π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for every place v. In particular the central character of π is det ρ (read through geometric reciprocity), and for every quasi-character χ of C_F and every place v the local factors agree: L(s, π_v⊗χ_v) = L(s, ρ_v⊗χ_v) and ε(s, π_v⊗χ_v, ψ_v) = ε(s, ρ_v⊗χ_v, ψ_v); in particular L(s, π⊗χ) = L(s, ρ⊗χ) for the completed L-functions, which are therefore entire when ρ is irreducible. The archimedean hypothesis cannot be dropped from this argument: it is what lets the archimedean factors cancel (Langlands's unproved Lemma 3.2 would be needed otherwise).
hypotheses: F is a number field; ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) is continuous (finite image); π is cuspidal automorphic on GL₂(A_F).

π(ρ_v) uses the unitary correspondence rec of R16.3 (AF.1 at infinity), with geometric reciprocity, unshifted standard factors and det rec(π_v) corresponding to the central character. Do not use recᵀ = rec ⊗ ν⁻¹/² here: it shifts the L-variable and determinant. Since ρ_v has bounded image and N = 0, its unitary correspondent is tempered and generic.
T is a finite set of finite places; π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for all finite v ∉ T and all archimedean v.
proofSteps: Central characters. ω_π and det ρ (a quasi-character of C_F by reciprocity) agree at every v ∉ T, because the correspondence matches central characters with determinants. Their quotient is a Hecke character trivial on F_v^× for all v ∉ T; as F^× is dense in ∏_{v ∈ T}F_v^× (weak approximation), it is trivial. Hence ω_{π_v} = det ρ_v for every v, including v ∈ T.

Fix v₀ ∈ T and a quasi-character χ₀ of F_{v₀}^×. For each v ∈ T∖{v₀}, gl2-twist-stability applied to π_v and π(ρ_v), which have the same central character by the first step, gives a bound m_v. isolating-twist-character supplies ω on C_F with ω_{v₀} = χ₀ and c(ω_v) > m_v for v ∈ T∖{v₀}.

π⊗ω is cuspidal, so its completed L-function satisfies the functional equation of R16.5/global-epsilon-normalization with ε the product of local ε-factors (JL70 Theorem 11.1, p. 179); ρ⊗ω satisfies artin-twisted-functional-equation with the same additive character ψ. At every v ∉ T the local L- and ε-factors of π_v⊗ω_v and ρ_v⊗ω_v coincide (hypothesis and the factor compatibilities of R16.3, including R16.3/archimedean-factor-comparison at infinity). Dividing the two functional equations by the common partial L-functions gives ∏_{v ∈ T} γ(s, π_v⊗ω_v, ψ_v) = ∏_{v ∈ T} γ(s, ρ_v⊗ω_v, ψ_v) as meromorphic functions (JL70 p. 210). In R16.5 undo the conductor factor A(π⊗ω)^{s/2} in its completion before forming the product of the raw local constants. For nonunitary ω use the real norm-power shift; this also extends the unitary statement of AL.2/global-godement-jacquet.

For v ∈ T∖{v₀}, γ(s, ρ_v⊗ω_v, ψ_v) = γ(s, π(ρ_v)⊗ω_v, ψ_v) by R16.3, and this equals γ(s, π_v⊗ω_v, ψ_v) by gl2-twist-stability. Cancelling leaves γ(s, π_{v₀}⊗χ₀, ψ_{v₀}) = γ(s, π(ρ_{v₀})⊗χ₀, ψ_{v₀}) for the arbitrary χ₀.

π_{v₀} is infinite-dimensional (local components of cuspidal representations are generic: R16.4/global-whittaker-expansion), as is π(ρ_{v₀}); their central characters agree; gl2-local-converse gives π_{v₀} ≅ π(ρ_{v₀}). The factor identities follow from R16.3; the global identity follows, and for irreducible ρ the twisted L-functions are entire because L(s, π⊗χ) is the standard L-function of a cuspidal representation of GL₂ (AL.2/global-godement-jacquet).
acceptance: For a dihedral ρ = Ind_{G_K}^{G_F} θ the conclusion recovers the all-place local components of quadratic automorphic induction (JL70 Proposition 12.1), where T can be taken empty.
With T = {v₀} the stability step is vacuous and the conclusion is the local converse theorem applied to the single quotient of functional equations.

If the archimedean components were not known to match, the quotient of functional equations would contain archimedean γ-factors that highly ramified finite twists do not control; the hypothesis is used, not decorative.
Weak matching at almost all places with π not cuspidal (π = π(μ, ν) isobaric, ρ = μ⊕ν) is outside the statement; that case is settled directly by Hecke characters.
For an unramified character pair with Frobenius eigenvalues α,β, the local factor is ((1−αq⁻ˢ)(1−βq⁻ˢ))⁻¹ and the central character at a uniformiser is αβ. There is no extra q or half-integral shift.

sources.match: Jacquet and Langlands isolate the places of a finite set S one at a time by a twist with prescribed component at one place and high ramification at the others, use Proposition 3.8 and the corresponding Galois-side stability to cancel the other places, and conclude from the resulting identity of local factors; here the cuspidal representation is given and the Galois side is compared through the local correspondence, so only GL₂ stability is needed.

nodes.title: Tetrahedral Artin automorphy at every place
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field and ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) continuous, irreducible, with projective image A₄, and let π be the cuspidal representation of R17.5/tetrahedral-artin (the cubic descent of the dihedral π(ρ_E), with ω_π = det ρ). Then π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) at every place v of F, including the archimedean ones and the places dividing 2 where ρ_v may be primitive. In particular all twisted L- and ε-factors of π and ρ agree at every place. At an archimedean v the component is π(1, 1) if ρ(c_v) = 1, π(sgn, sgn) if ρ(c_v) = −1 and the weight-one limit π(1, sgn) if ρ(c_v) is a non-scalar involution; at a complex v it is π(1, 1).
hypotheses: F is a number field; ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) is continuous and irreducible with projective image A₄.
E/F is the cyclic cubic extension cut out by the preimage of the normal subgroup V₄ ⊂ A₄; P = ρ|_{W_E} is dihedral, and π(P) is its quadratic automorphic induction (R17.5/dihedral-artin).
π is the cyclic descent of π(P) to F with ω_π = det ρ constructed in R17.5/tetrahedral-artin; it satisfies π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for almost all v.
proofSteps: Archimedean places. Every archimedean v of F splits completely in E: the decomposition group at v has order at most 2 inside Gal(E/F) ≅ Z/3. For w | v, E_w = F_v, and R17.4/cyclic-base-change gives BC_{E/F}(π)_w ≅ π_v at the split place. By construction BC_{E/F}(π) ≅ π(P) (R17.4/cyclic-descent), and π(P)_w ≅ π(P_w) at every place by quadratic induction (R17.5/quadratic-induction, JL70 Proposition 12.1). As P_w = ρ|_{W_{E_w}} = ρ_v, π_v ≅ π(ρ_v).

The explicit archimedean components: ρ(W_C) is trivial (a connected group maps trivially to the profinite G_F), so ρ_v is a sum of characters of W_R/C^× ≅ {±1} determined by ρ(c_v), and AF.1/archimedean-llc-gln gives the listed principal series.
Finite places. R17.5/tetrahedral-artin gives π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) outside a finite set T of finite places. artin-all-place-upgrade, with the archimedean matching just proved, extends this to every place.
acceptance: If the image of ρ is the binary tetrahedral group, whose only involution is −1, then ρ(c_v) is scalar at every real v and π_v is π(1, 1) or π(sgn, sgn); an odd tetrahedral ρ over Q (det ρ(c) = −1) has a non-scalar involution in its image and π_∞ is the weight-one limit π(1, sgn).

At an unramified place inert in E, R17.5/tetrahedral-artin removes a cube-root-of-unity ambiguity in the Satake class by a group-theoretic argument; at the finitely many places that argument does not reach (places ramified for ρ, in particular those over 2 where ρ_v can be primitive) only artin-all-place-upgrade identifies π_v.

Replacing π by π⊗η with η the cubic character of E/F gives a representation with the same base change to E but different central character; it is not π(ρ), so the determinant normalisation of R17.5/tetrahedral-artin is essential.

nodes.title: Octahedral Artin automorphy at every place
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field and ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) continuous, irreducible, with projective image S₄, and let π be the cuspidal representation of R17.5/octahedral-artin (Tunnell's choice among the two quadratic descents of the tetrahedral representation of ρ|_{G_E}, E/F the quadratic field of the preimage of A₄). Then π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) at every place v of F. At a real place v that is complex in E, ρ(c_v) is a non-scalar involution (its projective image is a transposition), ρ_v = 1⊕sgn and π_v is the weight-one limit π(1, sgn); at real places split in E and at complex places the component is read off from the tetrahedral representation over E.
hypotheses: F is a number field; ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) is continuous and irreducible with projective image S₄.
E/F is the quadratic extension cut out by the preimage of A₄; ρ_E = ρ|_{G_E} has projective image A₄; π_E is its tetrahedral cuspidal representation (tetrahedral-artin-all-places over E).
π is the quadratic descent of π_E singled out by Tunnell's lemma in R17.5/octahedral-artin, with π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for almost all v.
proofSteps: Central character. As in artin-all-place-upgrade, ω_π = det ρ, since both agree at almost all places.

Archimedean v split in E, and complex v: for w | v, E_w = F_v and BC_{E/F}(π)_w ≅ π_v (R17.4/cyclic-base-change); BC_{E/F}(π) ≅ π_E because π is a quadratic descent of π_E, which matches ρ_E at every place of E by tetrahedral-artin-all-places applied over E; so π_v ≅ π(ρ_v).

Real v with E_w = C: ρ(c_v) lies outside the preimage of A₄, so its projective image is an odd involution of S₄, a transposition; hence ρ(c_v) is a non-scalar involution, det ρ(c_v) = −1 and ρ_v = 1⊕sgn. By R17.4/local-compatibility the parameter φ of π_v restricts to W_C as the parameter of BC_{E/F}(π)_w = π_{E,w} = π(1, 1), so φ is trivial on C^× and φ ∈ {1⊕1, 1⊕sgn, sgn⊕sgn}. Its determinant is ω_{π_v} = det ρ_v, which is sgn; only 1⊕sgn has determinant sgn, so π_v ≅ π(1, sgn) = π(ρ_v).
Finite places: artin-all-place-upgrade with the archimedean matching just proved.

The weak octahedral input has been collated against Tunnell pp. 173–175 in the archived AMS scan with the original hash. The p. 174 lemma chooses between two quadratic descents by non-normal cubic base change, not by determinant matching. The p. 175 Satake calculation excludes projective order 6. The JPSS transfer remains imported from R17.3’s R17.4a/AL.3b supplier plan; source collation does not replace that analytic proof.
acceptance: For F = Q and ρ = s∘r̄ with r̄: G_Q → GL₂(F₃) odd and surjective (R17.5/octahedral-mod-three-application), E is the quadratic field cut out by det r̄, which is imaginary because det r̄(c) = −1; the real place is complex in E and π_∞ is the weight-one limit π(1, sgn).

The two descents π₁ and π₂ = π₁⊗ω_{E/F} have the same central character and the same base change to E; at a real place complex in E they have the same archimedean component as well (twisting by ω_{E/F} sends π(1, sgn) to π(sgn, 1) ≅ π(1, sgn)), so archimedean matching does not choose between them: Tunnell's cubic comparison does.
The archimedean step uses only the quadratic descent and the central character; Tunnell's cubic comparison and the upgrade are still needed at the finite places.

nodes.title: The Brauer character of a modular representation
nodes.statement: Let Γ be a finite group, p a prime, k an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, m ≥ 1 an integer prime to p that is divisible by the order of every p-regular element of Γ (for instance the prime-to-p part of the exponent of Γ), and τ: μ_m(k) → μ_m(C) a group isomorphism. For a representation r: Γ → GL_n(k) and a p-regular g ∈ Γ (order prime to p), r(g) is diagonalisable and its eigenvalues λ₁, …, λ_n, counted with algebraic multiplicity, lie in μ_m(k). The Brauer character of r is the complex-valued function on the p-regular elements φ_r(g) = τ(λ₁) + … + τ(λ_n). It depends on τ, is defined only on p-regular elements, and is not a lift of the trace of r(g) ∈ k (Webb's Example 10.1.2 has trace 1 and Brauer character −1). For a representation over a subfield k₀ ⊂ k (for example a finite field) one takes the Brauer character of its extension of scalars to k. The suggested matrix function is total on Γ: it sums the τ-lifts of characteristic-polynomial roots, assigning 0 to a root outside μ_m. Its restriction to p-regular elements is the Brauer character; all character-theoretic identities below are asserted on that restriction.
hypotheses: Γ is a finite group and p is prime; k is algebraically closed of characteristic p.
m is prime to p and divisible by the order of every p-regular element of Γ; τ: μ_m(k) ≅ μ_m(C) is an isomorphism of cyclic groups of order m.
r: Γ → GL_n(k) is a group homomorphism (equivalently a finite-dimensional kΓ-module with a basis); φ_r is defined on {g ∈ Γ : gcd(ord g, p) = 1}.
proofSteps: For g p-regular, r(g)^{ord g} = 1 and ord g is prime to p, so X^{ord g} − 1 is separable over k; r(g) is diagonalisable with eigenvalues in μ_{ord g}(k) ⊂ μ_m(k) (Webb §10.1, before Example 10.1.2).
Define φ_r(g) as the sum of τ over the roots of the characteristic polynomial of r(g), with multiplicity; this is independent of any ordering and of the basis.

For a p-modular system (F, R, k) with F of characteristic zero containing μ_m, reduction modulo the maximal ideal is an isomorphism μ_m(R) → μ_m(k) (Webb Lemma 10.1.1; R01.1/reduction-of-roots-of-unity proves it for the algebraic closure of Q_p); choosing τ as the composite of its inverse with an embedding F → C makes the Brauer character of a reduced lattice equal to the ordinary character (API brauerCharacter_reduction).

The root-of-unity comparison for a general splitting p-modular system uses Webb Lemma 10.1.1: X^m−1 has distinct roots modulo p since p ∤ m. The R01.1/reduction-of-roots-of-unity node covers the p-adic algebraic-closure instance, not every domain in the comparison API.
acceptance: The listed tests hold, and the API items listed above are consistent with Webb Proposition 10.1.3 (1)–(6).
brauerCharacter agrees with the ordinary character of any integral lift on p-regular elements, which is the property used by brauer-character-recognition and fong-swan.

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter
api.statement: The function on p-regular elements g ↦ Σ τ(λᵢ), the sum over the eigenvalues of r(g) with algebraic multiplicity, for fixed p, m, τ.

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_spectrum
api.statement: If the characteristic polynomial of r(g) is ∏ᵢ (X − aᵢ) with aᵢ ∈ μ_m(k), then φ_r(g) = Σᵢ τ(aᵢ).

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_one
api.statement: φ_r(1) = n, the dimension, as a complex number (Webb 10.1.3(1)).

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_conjugate
api.statement: φ_r(xgx⁻¹) = φ_r(g) for all x ∈ Γ: a class function on p-regular classes (Webb 10.1.3(2)).

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_conj_equiv
api.statement: If r′(g) = P r(g) P⁻¹ for a fixed P ∈ GL_n(k), then φ_{r′} = φ_r: the Brauer character depends only on the isomorphism class.

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_inv
api.statement: φ_r(g⁻¹) is the complex conjugate of φ_r(g) and equals the Brauer character of the dual representation at g (Webb 10.1.3(3)).

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_tensor
api.statement: The Brauer character of the tensor product (Kronecker product of matrices) is the product φ_r·φ_{r′} (Webb 10.1.3(4)).

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_blockTriangular
api.statement: If r is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks r₁ and r₂, then φ_r = φ_{r₁} + φ_{r₂}; hence φ is additive in short exact sequences and depends only on composition factors with multiplicity (Webb 10.1.3(5)).

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_reduction
api.statement: Let R be a domain, f: R → k a ring map and σ: R → C an injective ring map with τ(f(ζ)) = σ(ζ) for every ζ ∈ μ_m(R). Assume that charpoly(ρ(g)) splits in R as ∏ᵢ(X−ζᵢ), ζᵢ ∈ μ_m(R). For ρ: Γ → GL_n(R) and p-regular g, the Brauer character of f∘ρ at g equals σ(tr ρ(g)), the ordinary character (Webb 10.1.3(6)). This splitting hypothesis is explicit in the Lean statement; a general domain need not contain these eigenvalues.

api.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_mapField
api.statement: For an embedding of algebraically closed fields k → k′ and τ′ restricting to τ, the Brauer character of the extended representation equals φ_r.

tests.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_rank_one_test
tests.statement: For n = 1 and r(g) = a ∈ μ_m(k), φ_r(g) = τ(a).

tests.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_cube_root_test
tests.statement: For g of order 3 acting with eigenvalues a and a² where τ(a) is a primitive cube root of unity (for instance the F₂-matrix with rows (0, 1) and (1, 1)), φ_r(g) = −1, although the trace of r(g) in characteristic 2 is 1; lifting the trace would give the wrong value.

tests.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_identity_rank_p_test
tests.statement: The trivial representation of rank p has φ(1) = p ≠ 0 in C, although its trace in k is 0: the Brauer character remembers the dimension.

tests.name: TauCeti.GL2Transfer.brauerCharacter_sign_reduction_test
tests.statement: For Γ of order 2, p = 3 and the sign representation over Z reduced to F₃, the Brauer character at the generator is −1, the value of the ordinary character.

nodes.title: Brauer characters determine composition factors
nodes.statement: Let Γ be finite, k algebraically closed of characteristic p, and φ the Brauer character for a fixed τ. (a) The Brauer characters of the simple kΓ-modules S₁, …, S_r are linearly independent over C and form a basis of the class functions on p-regular conjugacy classes; the Brauer characters of their projective covers P_{S₁}, …, P_{S_r} form the dual basis for the pairing ⟨α, β⟩ = |Γ|⁻¹ Σ_{g p-regular} α(g⁻¹)β(g), with ⟨φ_{P_{S_i}}, φ_{S_j}⟩ = δ_{ij}. (b) Two finite-dimensional kΓ-modules have the same Brauer character if and only if they have the same composition factors with the same multiplicities; in particular a module whose Brauer character equals that of a simple module S is isomorphic to S. (c) Let (F, R, k₀) be a p-modular system with F of characteristic zero containing the m-th roots of unity, uniformiser ϖ, k₀ ⊂ k, and τ compatible with reduction of roots of unity and an embedding F → C. For a full RΓ-lattice L in an FΓ-module V, the Brauer character of (L/ϖL) ⊗_{k₀} k is the ordinary character of V restricted to p-regular elements; different full lattices give reductions with the same composition factors (Brauer–Nesbitt).
hypotheses: Γ finite; k algebraically closed of characteristic p (a splitting field for Γ); τ as in R17.5/brauer-character.

In (c): R is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser ϖ, fraction field F of characteristic zero containing μ_m, and residue field k₀ ⊂ k; τ(ζ mod ϖ) = σ(ζ) for ζ ∈ μ_m(R) and a fixed embedding σ: F → C.
proofSteps: (c) For p-regular g, the eigenvalues of g on V lie in μ_m(F) ⊂ R and reduce to the eigenvalues on L/ϖL, so the two sums agree under τ (Webb Proposition 10.1.3(6) with Lemma 10.1.1). Brauer–Nesbitt for lattices (Webb Theorem 9.4.8; R01.1/brauer-nesbitt for the characteristic-polynomial form) gives the independence of the lattice.

Projective covers come from QuiverRepresentations Layer 3. GrothendieckEulerForms Layer 4 gives dim Hom(P_S,T)=δ_ST in the split setting. projective-brauer-hom identifies this with the Brauer pairing. brauer-class-count gives equality between the number of simples and the dimension of p-regular class functions. Thus the two finite families are dual bases (Webb 10.2.2).

(b) Brauer characters are additive in short exact sequences (R17.5/brauer-character, API brauerCharacter_blockTriangular), so φ_U = Σ_S [U : S] φ_S; by (a) the multiplicities [U : S] are determined by φ_U (Webb Corollary 10.2.3(3)). If φ_U = φ_S for simple S, U has a single composition factor S and so U ≅ S.
acceptance: Webb's Example 10.1.2: the two-dimensional F₂C₃-module U (simple over F₂) becomes, over k, the sum of the two nontrivial characters; its Brauer character at the generator is −1, while two trivial factors give 2 and a trivial plus a nontrivial factor give 1 + ζ with ζ a primitive cube root of unity, so the composition factors are read off from the value.

In characteristic p, the regular representation of a cyclic p-group has the same Brauer character (|Γ| at 1) as |Γ| copies of the trivial module but is not semisimple: (b) determines composition factors, not the module.
(c) for Γ of order prime to p recovers the bijection between simple modules in characteristic zero and in characteristic p (Webb Theorem 9.4.11, p. 155).

sources.match: Brauer characters are additive in short exact sequences, depend only on composition factors, and equal the ordinary character of a lift on p-regular elements.
